newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour victory seen hurting Saatchi brothers.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour victory seen hurting Saatchi brothers.

text.p: The landslide election victory by Britain's Labour Party over the Conservatives on Thursday is expected to tarnish the reputation of advertising gurus Maurice and Charles Saatchi, industry experts said on Friday.

Many advertising executives and others say the Saatchi brothers helped bring former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher to power in 1979 and helped the Tories win three subsequent elections with powerful advertising.

Experts told Reuters they did not consider the Saatchis and their ad agency, M&C Saatchi, responsible for the Tory's resounding drubbing in Thursday's general election, but said the Saatchis' reputation would suffer nonetheless.
Even before voters went to the polls, rumours were rife in the advertising industry that the Conservatives would seek a new ad agency after the election.
"To be associated with this campaign will not do M&C Saatchi any favours," one advertising executive told Reuters.
He said it helped any ad agency to be linked with success, and, similarly, association with failure cast a shadow over an agency.

Maurice and Charles Saatchi built advertising fame after creating Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising in 1970. In December 1994 they left the agency after losing a boardroom battle and went on to create M&C Saatchi.
Prime Minister John Major made Maurice Saatchi a Lord in August 1996 in a move that pleased ad executives and angered the opposition Labour Party.
The Saatchi brothers' creation of a famous "Labour Isn't Working" poster ad in 1979 was a turning point for political advertising in Britain.
Prior to 1979, many British politicians failed to understand the powerful role advertising could play in an election campaign.
"It's a very American thing to market a politician," Ron Zeghibe, chief executive of British outdoor advertising concern Maiden Group Plc , told Reuters.
The Tories in 1979, learning from the U.S. presidential campaign then being mounted by Ronald Reagan, hand-picked a team of advertisers rather than hire an agency.
The new team of backroom strategists included the Saatchis and Sir Tim Bell, a media and public relations expert.

In devising the "Labour Isn't Working" poster -- which showed a long queue of people outside an unemployment office -- the ad team captured the mood of a country crippled by unemployment and labour strikes in a period that has become known as the "winter of discontent."
Before 1979, many ad agencies were wary of handling political accounts because politicians were considered difficult to work with and strong political opinions could cause rifts within ad agencies.
"What changed all that was the huge success that Saatchi had when the Conservatives came to power in 1979," Hugh Burkitt, of the Court, Burkitt & Co. ad agency, said.
The 1979 ad campaign, followed by the Saatchi 1983 campaign for the Tories, "all added to the magic luster and success of Saatchi & Saatchi," Burkitt said.
Now the Labour landslide will likely have an opposite effect -- although it is expected to be more subtle.
"There could be a bit of an inverse effect," Burkitt said. "This will make top line clients more wary," he said, noting that many establishment clients already have shied away from the Saatchis.
"There will be a belief that the advertising could have been more effective," said Anthony de Larrinaga, a media analyst at Panmure Gordon.

Advertising executives and political experts had been critical of the ads run by both parties in recent months. Despite record spending, the advertising has been criticised as dull and for failing to crystalise issues.
Infighting in the Conservative Party and an inability of party officials to agree on campaign issues made it difficult for advertising creatives to deliver a clear message.
"There was no right message," said Maiden's Zeghibe. "If that's the reality, how can you build an argument that it's their fault?"

But while the Saatchis' reputation may suffer, advertising executives said there will be no turning back by politicians in widespread use of advertising in future campaigns -- and no lack of agencies eager to do the work.
"I think there will be a lot of agencies falling over themselves to do the (Tories') business," one ad executive said.
